commitResults.messageTitle: Level-0: Rename Duke to Aster and greet
Level-3: Add task status with Task class
Level-4: Add typed tasks with inheritance
Level-5: Handle input errors with exceptions
Level-7: Add task storage and file format
commitResults.messageBody:
Tasks are lost when Aster exits because they exist only in memory.

Add a plain-text format for every task type and preserve each task's
status and type-specific fields. Escape separators in user text so
saved tasks can be read back without changing their contents.

Ignore generated data so personal task lists are not committed.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-7: Save and reload tasks on disk
commitResults.messageBody:
Aster keeps its task list only for the duration of one run.

Load saved tasks before accepting commands and save the list after each
successful change. Stop safely when existing data cannot be read so a
possibly recoverable file is not overwritten.

Level-7 is complete on its required development branch.

Merge it without fast-forwarding so the branch topology remains visible
for course verification.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-8: Store deadlines and events as dates
commitResults.messageBody:
Deadline and event dates were kept as whatever text the user typed, so
Aster could not tell a real date from any other words and could not
show one in a friendlier form.

Hold them as LocalDate instead, accept them as yyyy-MM-dd, and show
them as MMM dd yyyy with an explicit English locale so the output does
not change with the machine. Text that is not a real date is now
refused, which also rules out impossible dates such as 2019-02-29.

Store dates in ISO form so the data file stays locale independent. A
stored date that cannot be read is treated like any other unreadable
record: Aster explains and stops without overwriting the file.

Level-8 is complete on its required development branch.

Merge it without fast-forwarding so the branch topology remains visible
for course verification.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-MoreOOP: Split Aster into focused classes
commitResults.messageBody:
Aster held the only Scanner, every println, the command switch, the
parsing helpers and the task list itself, so no single responsibility
had a clear home and the class had grown past 400 lines.

Move user interaction into Ui, command interpretation into Parser, and
the task collection into TaskList, beside the Storage class that was
already separate. Storage is reused unchanged, so persistence behavior
is untouched.

Give each action its own Command object, with the keyword enum renamed
to CommandType to free the name while keeping its role as the single
list of keywords. A command that changes the list requests a save
after the change has been applied and reported. Checks that refuse a
command run before anything is changed. Aster retains only the run
loop.

Task numbers are still resolved against the list at execution time, so
the existing checks keep their order and their messages.

No user-visible behavior changes: the same transcript produces the
same output and the same data file as before.

A-MoreOOP is complete on its development branch.

Merge it without fast-forwarding to preserve the completed branch
topology while keeping master at the verified implementation.

Every class sat in the default package, which the Java coding standard
does not allow and which left nineteen unrelated files in one flat
folder with nothing to show how they fit together.

Give each class a package that matches the responsibility it was given
in the previous increment: aster for the entry point, and aster.command,
aster.parser, aster.storage, aster.task, aster.ui and aster.exception
for the rest. The folders now mirror the packages, and src/main/java
stays the source root.

Each file now states what it depends on, and those dependencies were
checked to run in one direction only. Two members that no longer need
to be reachable from outside their own package were narrowed to suit.

No user-visible behavior changes: the same transcript produces the same
output and the same data file as before.

A-Packages is complete on its development branch.

Merge it without fast-forwarding to preserve the completed branch
topology while keeping master at the verified packaged implementation.

Bring in the Gradle wrapper and build script supplied by the course on
the add-gradle-support branch, providing the project's Gradle build
foundation.

The supplied script still names the template entry point, so a focused
follow-up change will connect the run task to this project's packaged
Aster entry point.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-Gradle: Run the app through Gradle
commitResults.messageBody:
The supplied build script names seedu.duke.Duke as the application main
class, which is the template's entry point and does not exist here. Point
it at aster.Aster instead, so that the run task starts this chatbot.

This is the only change the merged build script needs: src/main/java is
already the source root the java plugin expects, and the packaged sources
under aster/ are found without further configuration.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-JUnit: Add JUnit tests for storage and dates
commitResults.messageBody:
Cover two high-risk areas where defects could reject, lose, or silently
change user data: Storage's save/load pair, which implements the on-disk
format, and TaskDates' parsing and display formatting.

Storage is tested through save/load round trips and hand-written
malformed records, so both halves of the format are checked through
observable behaviour rather than a restated copy of the implementation.
Every filesystem test uses a JUnit temporary directory, so the real data
file is never touched.

No production source or build configuration changes are needed because
the Gradle JUnit setup inherited with A-Gradle already matches the course
tutorial.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-Jar: Name the distributed JAR after Aster
commitResults.messageBody:
Shadow was producing build/libs/duke.jar, a name inherited from the
course's add-gradle-support branch and left over from the Duke template
this project started as. The chatbot has been Aster since Level-0, and
the JAR is the only artifact a user actually downloads and runs, so it
was the last place the old name was still visible.

Setting archiveFileName to Aster.jar makes the distributed file match
the program inside it, and makes the documented run command read
java -jar "Aster.jar". Nothing about the build or the program changes.

commitResults.messageTitle: A-JavaDoc: Document the last undocumented parts
commitResults.messageBody:
Javadoc coverage was already complete for everything that declares
itself, but three gaps remained. Six parameter and return descriptions
in the oldest three classes end without a period while every other
class's do not. One private enum constructor says nothing about the
value it stores. Command and ListCommand declare no constructor at
all, so Java generates one that reaches the published API with no
comment on it, which doclint reports as a warning.

Punctuate those descriptions, document the enum constructor, and give
the two classes an explicit constructor to hang a comment on, so the
generated pages read uniformly and javadoc -Xdoclint:all is silent.
Nothing executes differently; the 34 existing tests still pass.

The coding standard requires American spelling. Three places still
read "recognise": two class comments and the message shown when a
command is not understood.

Spell all three the American way. The message the user sees changes
by one word; nothing else does.

The standard requires method names to be verbs, but CommandType
exposes keyword() and keywordList(), which read as nouns and so give
no hint that they are queries rather than fields. Two local booleans
in the parser read as verbs for the same reason.

Rename them to getKeyword(), getKeywordList(), isWordStart and
isWordEnd, and update the four call sites. Names only; no behaviour
changes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Level-9: Find tasks by description keyword
commitResults.messageBody:
A list that only grows becomes hard to search by eye, and the only way
to look something up is to read the whole list from the top.

Add a find command that shows the tasks whose description contains a
keyword, matched without regard to letter case so that a search does
not depend on how the task was typed. The filtering lives in TaskList,
beside the collection it reads, which keeps the command as thin as
list and lets the matching be tested without touching the screen or
the disk. Searching changes nothing, so find neither saves the list
nor creates the data file.

Matches are numbered across themselves rather than by their place in
the full list, which is what the increment's example shows; the
heading names what is being shown so the two cannot be confused.
